title: See competitors' TikTok ads in Europe, with targeting and reach, in Python
author: Aurelix Solutions
summary: Under the EU Digital Services Act, TikTok publishes the ads shown in the EU/EEA, Switzerland, the UK and Turkey in a public library: who ran it, who paid for it, when it ran, how many people saw it, and the targeting behind it, down to reach by country, age and gender. For a marketer that is a view into a competitor's TikTok strategy. The library is built for looking up one ad at a time, though, not for a table of every ad a brand ran this month or a morning list of what is new. This post pulls those ads into Python, builds a competitor sheet with targeting and reach, and sets up a daily "new ads only" watch. Disclosure: I'm Aurelix, and I built the TikTok Ads Library API . It's a paid tool (prices below). What each row holds One row per ad: ad_id , ad_library_url , format (video or image), industry , and removed when TikTok shows a removal reason. The advertiser: advertiser_name , advertiser_id , advertiser_registered_location , paid_for_by , and the linked TikTok account ( tiktok_business_account , tiktok_account_display_name , tiktok_business_account_followers , tiktok_account_url ). first_shown and last_shown (ISO 8601 UTC), and unique_users_seen as TikTok shows it ( 100K-200K ) plus unique_users_seen_range as numbers. ad_text , call_to_action , landing_url (the app-store link for app ads) and objective (Reach, Sales, Traffic and so on). video_urls , video_cover_urls and image_urls . targeting : regions , ages and genders per country, interests , audience_size , custom and excluded audiences, languages, devices and operating systems, and reach_by_region with reach per age and gender. Queries can be keywords ( "sneakers" ), advertiser names ( "Nike" , searched like a keyword) or Ad Library URLs copied from the browser. A URL that names one advertiser returns only that advertiser's ads. A competitor's ads as a sheet pip install apify-client import csv import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ " APIFY_TOKEN " ]) run = client . actor ( " aurelix/tiktok-ads-library-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " queries " : [ " sneakers " , " running shoes " ], " country " : " FR " , " days " : 30 , " maxResultsPerQuery " : 100 , " includeDetails " : True , } ) ads = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) fields = [ " advertiser_name " , " paid_for_by " , " first_shown " , " last_shown " , " unique_users_seen " , " objective " , " call_to_action " , " landing_url " , " ad_text " , " ad_library_url " ] with open ( " tiktok_ads.csv " , " w " , newline = "" , encoding = " utf-8 " ) as f : w = csv . DictWriter ( f , fieldnames = fields , extrasaction = " ignore " ) w . writeheader () w . writerows ( ads ) reach = {} for ad in ads : low = ( ad . get ( " unique_users_seen_range " ) or {}). get ( " min " ) or 0 reach [ ad [ " advertiser_name " ]] = reach . get ( ad [ " advertiser_name " ], 0 ) + low for name , users in sorted ( reach . items (), key = lambda x : - x [ 1 ])[: 10 ]: print ( f " { name [ : 40 ] : 40 } at least { users : > 12 , } users reached " ) The first file is the swipe file: every ad with its text, call to action and landing page. The second loop ranks advertisers by the low end of the reach TikTok reports, a quick read on who reaches the most people in that niche. Who the ads were aimed at from collections import Counter interests , ages = Counter (), Counter () for ad in ads : t = ad . get ( " targeting " ) or {} interests . update ( t . get ( " interests " ) or []) for country_ages in ( t . get ( " ages " ) or {}). values (): ages . update ( country_ages ) print ( " Top interests: " , interests . most_common ( 8 )) print ( " Age groups: " , ages . most_common ()) Each ad's targeting is read from its public detail page: the countries, ages, genders and interests it was aimed at, the estimated audience size, and reach_by_region , which splits the people reached by country, age and gender. Turn includeDetails off for a faster list without targeting at the same price per ad; details_loaded says which rows have the detail fields. New ads every morning run_input = { " queries " : [ " sneakers " , " https://library.tiktok.com/ads?region=FR&adv_biz_ids=... " ], " country " : " FR " , " days " : 7 , " maxResultsPerQuery " : 100 , " incremental " : True , " stateKey " : " fr-sneakers-watch " , " slackWebhookUrl " : " https://hooks.slack.com/services/... " , } With incremental on, the first run returns every matching ad. Each later run with the same stateKey skips ads an earlier run already returned, so a daily schedule pays only for new ones. Save the input as a task in the Apify Console, schedule it daily, and the Slack URL gets the count and the top 10 new ads; nothing is sent when a run finds nothing. webhookUrl posts the same digest as JSON to Zapier, Make or n8n. Use cases Competitor research : which products a competitor pushes on TikTok, with what message, aimed at whom, and for how long. Creative swipe files : ad text, call to action, landing page and video links for a category, refreshed weekly. Media planning : reach and audience size by country, age and gender to benchmark your own campaigns. Lead lists for agencies : businesses that actively advertise on TikTok in a market, with their landing pages. Why this tool Targeting and reach on every ad: countries, ages, genders, interests, audience size, and reach by country, age and gender. Several keywords, advertisers or Ad Library URLs in one run. Exact limits: ask for 50 ads per query, get and pay for at most 50. An all-in price with no platform usage on top, and a new-ads-only mode with a Slack or webhook digest. What it doesn't cover: ads shown only outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland, the UK and Turkey, because TikTok's library doesn't list them. Limits worth knowing TikTok's search shows at most about 5,000 ads per query, and it sometimes ends a result list early. The query is then marked PARTIAL in the run status and you pay only for the ads returned; split big searches by country or a shorter period. With targeting on, each ad needs its own detail page, so runs take about 2 seconds per ad. Video and image links are signed by TikTok and expire after a while; download creatives soon after the run. days goes back at most 365, because TikTok keeps ads in the library for a year after they last ran. The tool reads only what a logged-out visitor sees in TikTok's public ad library, never logs in and solves no CAPTCHAs. Advertiser names are returned as the library shows them. FAQ Do I need a TikTok account? No. The tool never logs in and needs no TikTok account. How do I get one exact advertiser's ads? Search the advertiser in TikTok's ad library, copy the page address (it contains adv_biz_ids ) and paste it into queries . A plain name such as Nike is searched like a keyword. Can I search every covered country at once? Yes: set country to all . Are duplicates charged? No. Each ad is returned once per run even when several queries find it, and with incremental on, ads from earlier runs are skipped and not charged. Can an AI agent use it? Yes, through Apify's MCP server or API: give queries and optional filters. Cost $1.40 per 1,000 ads, with or without the targeting summary, plus a $0.04 start fee per run at the default 2 GB of memory. The price is the same on every Apify plan, with no platform usage on top. Duplicate ads are never charged, and a search with no ads pays only the start fee. title: I checked every quote Claude's deep research cited. One wasn't what the source said.
author: Andri Darnius
summary: AI research tools are good at sounding sourced. Every paragraph ends with a link, every key point sits in quotation marks. I wanted to know how often those quotes are actually on the page they link to, so I checked them with code instead of trusting the model. The setup I asked Claude's deep-research skill a technical question: "SQLite WAL vs rollback journal for concurrent writes." It came back with a solid report: four parallel researchers, 30 sources, and 21 direct quotes. Then I pulled out every quote and the link that followed it, fetched each page, and checked whether the quoted words were really there. Matching ignored case, punctuation, line breaks and PDF formatting, but never the words themselves. The result 20 of 21 quotes were exact. One wasn't. The report quotes the SQLite forum as saying: "a VM has its own memory space" The thread never says that. The closest sentence is: "QEMU provides a private virtual memory space for its VM" The meaning is close. The quotation marks are wrong. It's a paraphrase presented as a quote, and nothing in the research process checks for that. To be fair to deep research: its report was excellent and broader than mine (more on that below). One soft misquote in 21 isn't a scandal. But it's the kind of error that survives review, because it sounds right. It's not just one tool I hit the same problem in my own research agent. In one run on HTTP/3 performance, the agent quoted two research papers: It wrote "advantageous **for * users that move."* The paper says "advantageous **in case of * users that move."* It wrote "QUIC's removal of HOL blocking…" The paper says "QUIC's removal of HOL * (head-of-line)** blocking…"* Both are close enough that a reader, or the model re-reading its own notes, would accept them. Why this happens The cause I found most surprising: when an agent "reads" a page, it often doesn't see the page. Many agent web-fetch tools pass the page through a smaller model and return a summary or an answer to a prompt. The agent then quotes from that summary. Quotes drift. PDFs are worse: many fetch tools can't extract them at all, so the agent quotes from memory or from a secondary source. Asking the model to double-check doesn't fix this. It checks against the same summary. What worked Two changes, both boring: Quote from the exact page text. Before quoting, fetch the raw page (or extract the PDF's text) and copy from that, not from a summary. Check every quote with code. After research, fetch each cited page once and match each quote word for word, as whole words, in order. A quote is either on the page or it isn't. When a quote isn't on the cited page, check the other pages in the same research. Often the quote is real but pinned to the wrong source. In one run the checker found a real SQLite quote attributed to wal.html that actually lives on pragma.html , and corrected the link instead of dropping it. Does the checker itself work? I stress-tested it: 40 real verified quotes, 30 of them deliberately damaged (two words swapped, a "not" removed, a number changed, the wrong page cited) plus 5 invented quotes and 10 left intact. It classified 45 of 45 correctly. PDFs needed their own fixes. Footnote numbers glue onto words ("users1 ."), words split across lines ("trans-\nactions"), and ligatures replace letter pairs. Each one caused a false "not found" until handled. What it costs On the same SQLite question, my pipeline's research phase used 78,517 tokens on Claude Haiku . Deep research's four researchers used 278,826 on the main model . That's about 28% of the tokens, on a cheaper model. The trade-off is real: deep research found things mine didn't, including a SQLite WAL corruption bug fixed in 3.51.3 (March 2026) and corruption across Docker Desktop VM boundaries. Broader search costs more. Checking quotes costs almost nothing, since it's a script, not a model. Try it I packaged this as an agent skill called Quoteproof : a 5-angle research pipeline that quotes from exact page text and checks every quote before writing the report. The report ends with an audit line: quotes checked, verified, corrected, dropped. Free, MIT: Quoteproof Community checks quotes from web pages: git clone https://github.com/andre-arc/Quoteproof-Community.git ~/.claude/skills/quoteproof-community Pro: adds PDFs and research papers, exact-text quoting, and wrong-page detection: Agensi . All the data behind this post, including the deep research report and every quote checked: github.com/andre-arc/Quoteproof Tested with Claude Code. One limit to know: it proves a quote exists on the page, not that the page is right . I'm looking for reviewers So far every test is mine. I'd like researchers and programmers to try it on their own questions and tell me what happened, especially when it fails. Install the free edition (one git clone , above). Ask your agent to research something you know well, so you can judge the answer. Share the result in the comments here, or through the review form : what you researched, the audit line at the end of the report, anything it caught, and anything it got wrong. I'll read every response and publish a follow-up with what reviewers found, good and bad. With your permission, I'll quote you. Disclosure: I built Quoteproof and earn from sales of the Pro edition. The Agensi link is my referral link.

title: 26 AI Breakdowns of the Same 10-Second Reel: One Hook, 25 Different Topics
author: Matvey
summary: I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them takes a public Instagram Reel apart into a reusable script: the hook and why it works, the beats with what is on screen in each one, the call to action, and a fill-in template. It is not a transcript tool with a summary bolted on. The model gets frames sampled from the video — one every 2 seconds, 360 px wide, at most 12 — plus our own speech-to-text and the caption, and it answers in JSON. Which means half the output is an enum and half is prose written fresh each time. I have been quietly collecting evidence on what that costs, because like every Actor I publish, this one has a scheduled check: once a day, send one fixed Reel, make sure rows come out. Sixteen days of that check, 24 October to 8 November 2026, gave me 26 breakdowns of the same 10.4-second Reel — same model ( deepseek-flash ), same prompt, JSON mode, no temperature set, so the provider default applies. The Reel is a brow artist walking past a building: three lines of text burned into the picture, a trending song on the audio, 🔗 Link in bio to book in the caption. Each row cost $0.0506. If you are about to put LLM output into a database column, this is the field-by-field answer to "how much of it is stable". What never moved Field Across 26 runs ai.hook.source on-screen — 26/26 ai.onScreenText the same three lines, byte for byte — 26/26 ai.speechIsSong true — 26/26 ai.hook.text Some people call me Kara — 25/26 ai.hook.type statement — 25/26 first beat label hook — 25/26 last beat end 10.4 — 26/26 That is a better result than I expected, and it is the useful half of the finding. The model's judgement — where the hook lives, what it says, whether the audio is a song — is near-deterministic. The one run that disagreed on hook.text returned Some people call me Kara / Some people call me Kara Ann , which is the same hook with the second line glued on, not a different reading. What moved, and it is the fields you were going to filter on The beat count flipped. Four beats in 14 runs, three in 12. The labels behind those counts came back as ten distinct sequences : hook, setup, cta 5 runs hook, setup, value, outro 4 hook, setup, twist, outro 3 hook, setup, value, cta 3 hook, setup, twist, cta 3 hook, setup, twist 3 hook, value, cta 2 hook, value, outro 1 hook, setup, cta, outro 1 setup, setup, cta 1 Same ten seconds of video. Is the middle of it a setup , a value or a twist ? The model has no strong opinion, and neither would I. Fifteen of the 26 runs contained a beat labelled cta ; eleven did not. The boundaries moved too — 17 distinct sets of end-seconds across 26 runs, though the first beat ended at 3.0 s in 17 of them and the hook window never stretched past 3.5 s. cta.type gave three answers to one caption. link_in_bio 19 times, book 6 times, other once. The caption says 🔗 Link in bio to book — it is genuinely both, and the enum forces a choice. Worse for anyone grouping by it, five runs picked the spoken line But you can call me when you want the best brows as the CTA text instead of the caption line. That is the practical warning. cta.type is exactly the field an agency dashboard groups by, and on a Reel where two readings are defensible it will move between runs for free. The prose never repeats, and that is not a bug Free-text field Distinct values in 26 runs ai.scriptTemplate 26 ai.hook.whyItWorks 26 ai.format 26 ai.topic 25 ai.audience 21 ai.emotion 10 ( Playful and confident 15 times) Two runs of the same Reel, sixteen days apart: 24 Oct topic: Brow artist personal branding / booking intro 8 Nov topic: Eyebrow artist personal-brand introduction in Greenville, SC, with a name-pun hook that lands on her brow services 24 Oct template: Some people call me [formal name]. Some people call me [nickname or full name]. But you can call me when you want the [your signature result / service]. 🔗 Link in bio to [booking action]. 📍[city] 8 Nov template: Some people call me [First name]. Some people call me [Full name]. But you can call me when you want the [best service / result you offer]. Both are correct. Neither is the same string. whyItWorks ranged from 141 to 366 characters and the placeholder count in the template ran from 3 to 8. So the rule I now follow, and would hand to anyone storing model output: Diff on enums, never on prose. A scheduled watch that re-reads a creator weekly and alerts on "the breakdown changed" will fire every single week if it compares topic or scriptTemplate . Compare hook.source , hook.type , cta.type , speechIsSong , and the on-screen lines. Do not GROUP BY ai.topic . Twenty-five labels for one video is not a taxonomy. Map to your own closed list, or group by hook.type and cta.type , closed lists of 8 and 10 values respectively. Treat prose as the thing a human reads once. whyItWorks and scriptTemplate are worth the money precisely because they are written for this Reel. Store them, show them, do not join on them. If you need one canonical answer, run it once and keep it. The Actor has an "only new videos" switch with named watch lists for this: re-running a Reel you already have buys a new opinion, not a correction. Why the AI layer exists at all: the transcript is often not the hook The same Actor also fills rule-based fields for free — hookText , ctaText , beats , wordsPerMinute — from the transcript and caption, no model involved. Across 11 distinct Reels I have real breakdowns for (10 Instagram, 1 TikTok; 10.4 s to 136 s; natgeo, zachking, Duolingo, two small businesses), the free hook and the AI hook pointed at different sources in 5 of 11 : Reel free hookSource ai.hook.source Why brow artist, 10 s speech on-screen the audio is a song; the transcript is lyrics natgeo pangolin, 19 s caption visual no speech at all — hook is [close-up of a scaly pangolin foraging in a rotting log] coffee shop, 12 s caption on-screen no speech; the hook is "So what brought you here?" typed on the frame natgeo, 15 s caption on-screen no speech; City, desert, mountains, or coast—which would you explore first? Duolingo TikTok, 10 s speech caption the speech is Japanese conversational filler Three of the eleven Reels transcribed to an empty string. A transcript-only tool returns nothing for those, and a hook heuristic reading the caption gets Presented by @Rolex. Nine of the eleven came back with on-screen lines in ai.onScreenText even though exact OCR was switched off — the model reads its frames for free. The free CTA detector found 4 CTAs in 11 Reels, one of them a mid-video sentence that is not a CTA; the AI found 7, including Which animal do you want to see next? (type comment ) — the last sentence of a 50-word natgeo caption that my keyword rules walked straight past. Where the two agree — a talking-head Reel with real speech — the free fields are fine and you can switch the model off and pay $0.003. It is the silent, text-on-screen Reel that needs the frames, and that is a large slice of Instagram. Calling it curl -X POST "https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/lergassy~instagram-reel-script-extractor/run-sync-get-dataset-items?token= $APIFY_TOKEN " \ -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ -d '{"videoUrls":["https://www.instagram.com/reel/DckEW9NNVsJ/"], "aiAnalysis":true,"includeOnScreenText":false}' Profiles work too ( "profiles":["natgeo"] , up to the 12 newest Reels Instagram shows logged out). Pricing is per event: $0.05 for the breakdown, $0.003 per Reel, $0.0015 per started 10 seconds of speech on the Free plan — the 10.4-second Reel above is $0.056 there and $0.0506 on ours. A breakdown that fails is not charged; the row arrives with the reason in aiError . The Actor is Instagram Reel Script Extractor ; if you only want words and timestamps, the transcript-only version is the same engine with the model off by default. When this is the wrong tool You need reproducible output. Everything above. Run once, store the row, treat a re-run as a second opinion. You need every burned-in line with timestamps. The frames give you the text, not when it appeared. That is the separate OCR switch at $0.06 per Reel. You think the model watched the video. It saw up to 12 stills and read our transcript. A fast cut, a gesture between frames, a sound effect — all invisible to it. You need verbatim evidence. Quoted speech comes from speech recognition, which mishears. The breakdown is a strong first draft, not a transcript of record. The whole measurement in this post is a GET over the run history of one Actor and forty lines of Python. If you ship anything that puts an LLM's JSON into a table, point it at one fixed input for two weeks and count the distinct values per column before you decide which ones get an index.

title: How to get job listings from SEEK New Zealand with an API (Python, Node or no code)
author: Big Man
summary: SEEK is New Zealand's biggest job board. If you want its listings in a spreadsheet, a database or an automation (a morning feed of new jobs in your region, salary benchmarking, or a list of companies hiring right now), copying ads by hand doesn't scale. This tutorial uses Seek NZ Job Scraper , an Apify actor I built that reads SEEK's own JSON search API for seek.co.nz. It needs no browser and no proxy, so a run takes seconds. The full examples are on GitHub: auto-actor/seek-nz-job-scraper . What people use it for A fresh list of jobs in one region every morning, pushed to a Google Sheet or Slack. Salary benchmarking by classification or region. Lists of companies that are hiring right now (the company field), for sales or recruiting. Input { "keywords" : "carpenter" , "where" : "Auckland" , "maxItems" : 50 } keywords and where work the way they do on seek.co.nz; maxItems caps the number of jobs. title: Pydantic: Catch Bad Data Before It Reaches Your Database
author: The Practical Developer
summary: A library lets members borrow books through a web form. One day, a member types -5 into the loan period field, another mistypes her email, and a third pastes an ISBN with a letter in it. The form saves all three loans without complaint. The reminder email bounces, the -5 loan shows as overdue, and nobody can find the book with the broken ISBN. The database stored what it was given. The problem is that nobody checked what was given first. That is the gap Pydantic fills. You describe the shape of the data once, as a Python class, and Pydantic checks every record against it before your code trusts it. What I would check before using it My judgement is that Pydantic is worth adding the moment your code receives data it did not create: a form submission, a JSON body from an API, a row read from a spreadsheet. Inside your own code, a model is extra ceremony. At a boundary, where the data comes from a stranger, it is the cheapest insurance you can buy. The first thing I would check is which version you are installing. Pydantic v2 is a rewrite of v1, with different syntax, and v1 tutorials will mislead you. Install v2 and read v2 docs only. The second check is the email field. Pydantic's EmailStr needs an extra package, or your model refuses to load, with an error saying email-validator is not installed. I hit exactly that error while preparing this post, and the fix is one install: pip install "pydantic[email]" . The third check is how strict the validation should be. By default Pydantic is forgiving: it converts the string "14" into the number 14, and the string "2026-11-09" into a real date. That is usually what you want from form data, but if you need strict types, say so explicitly with strict mode, or the coercion will hide sloppy input. The fourth check is the alternative. Plain dataclasses plus hand-written if statements do the same job for one form, but they scatter the rules across your code and never produce a useful error message. Marshmallow does similar work and is a fine choice if your project already uses it. The verdict: use Pydantic for data that crosses a boundary into Python code, especially forms and API payloads. That flips if the data never leaves your own code, or if your team already validates with another library and switching means rewriting working code. A library loan, checked end to end A Pydantic model is a small Python class that declares what a piece of data must look like: this field is an email, that field is a whole number between 1 and 30, this one is a date. You write it once, and you build a model instance from every record that comes in. Valid data passes through as a typed object, with strings already converted to numbers and dates. Invalid data is rejected with a list of exactly what was wrong, field by field, so the form can tell the member what to fix instead of saving a broken loan. The worked example is the library from the opening. A loan has a member name, a member email, a book ISBN, a loan period in days, and a loan date. The model says what each of those must be: the name must not be empty, the email must look like an email, the ISBN must be exactly 13 digits, the loan period must be a whole number from 1 to 30 days, and the loan date must be a real date. Here is the model and a valid loan, run with Python 3.12.3 and Pydantic 2.14.3: from datetime import date , timedelta from pydantic import BaseModel , EmailStr , Field class Loan ( BaseModel ): member_name : str = Field ( min_length = 1 ) member_email : EmailStr book_isbn : str = Field ( pattern = r " ^\d{13}$ " ) loan_days : int = Field ( gt = 0 , le = 30 ) loan_date : date loan = Loan ( member_name = " Ayesha Khan " , member_email = " ayesha@example.com " , book_isbn = " 9780134685991 " , loan_days = 14 , loan_date = " 2026-11-09 " , ) print ( " Loan accepted for " , loan . member_name ) print ( " Book ISBN: " , loan . book_isbn ) print ( " Loan days: " , loan . loan_days ) due = loan . loan_date + timedelta ( days = loan . loan_days ) print ( " Due back: " , due ) Running it gave this real output: Loan accepted for Ayesha Khan Book ISBN: 9780134685991 Loan days: 14 Due back: 2026-11-23 The due date is right: 9 November plus 14 days is 23 November. The loan date arrived as the string "2026-11-09" and became a real date object, so adding days to it works, and the rest of the code can trust the types. Now the part the tidy tutorials skip: something goes wrong. A web form sends every value as text, so the same loan arrives with the loan period as the string "-5", typed by a member who meant 5 and hit the wrong key. The model expects a number greater than zero, and Pydantic refuses the whole loan. The real output is: Loan rejected: 1 validation error for Loan loan_days Input should be greater than 0 [type=greater_than, input_value='-5', input_type=str] For further information visit https://errors.pydantic.dev/2.14/v/greater_than One problem, naming the exact field, the rule it broke, and the value that broke it. Nothing was saved, no reminder was scheduled for a loan that ends before it starts, and the form knows what to tell the member. The fix is to correct the data: the member meant 14 days, so the same payload with "14" in place of "-5" passes at once, and the string is converted to the number 14 before the checks run. Running the corrected payload gave: Loan accepted for Ayesha Khan Book ISBN: 9780134685991 Loan days: 14 Due back: 2026-11-23 The lesson: data from a form is text until proven otherwise, and a negative number is a valid integer that happens to be nonsense. A model that checks the range, not just the type, catches both problems in one place, before the database ever sees them. Common mistakes and how to fix them 1. Creating a model without catching ValidationError. Bad data raises a ValidationError, and an uncaught raise inside a request handler crashes the request. Fix it with try/except around the model call: show the errors when validation fails, carry on when it passes. 2. Leaving a required field out of the payload. A loan with no member_email fails with Field required [type=missing, ...] , naming the missing field. The fix is to mark the field optional with a default, or to check the form sends it. Do not invent a placeholder email to satisfy the model. 3. Assuming extra fields are rejected. Pydantic ignores unknown keys by default, so a loan with an extra notes field passes and the notes quietly vanish. If extra data should be an error, set model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid") on the model so unknown keys fail instead of disappearing. 4. Trusting a date string that looks right. The date "2026-13-40" fails with Input should be a valid date or datetime, month value is outside expected range of 1-12 , because there is no month 13. Let the model reject it and ask for a real date, rather than parsing dates by hand. Where this leaves you Pydantic turns a hope into a check you can run: describe the data you expect, and every record gets measured against it before your code trusts it. It costs one small class per form or endpoint, and it pays that back the first time a mistyped email or a negative loan period is caught at the door instead of found in the database later. It will not fix a form that collects the wrong fields to begin with. The next step: pick one form in your own project, write a model for it, and feed it a bad payload. When the error points at the exact field, you will know whether your data needs a gatekeeper. title: Integrating India's GST e-Invoice IRP API: A Developer's Guide to IRN Generation in 2026
author: ZANISS SOFTWARES
summary: If you're building or maintaining billing software for the Indian market, you've probably hit the point where "just print an invoice" stopped being good enough. Since August 2023, any business crossing ₹5 crore in aggregate turnover has to get every B2B invoice registered with a government Invoice Registration Portal (IRP) before it's legally valid — and the integration details matter more than most teams expect going in. The flow itself is simple on paper: serialize your invoice into the prescribed JSON schema, POST it to an IRP or GSP endpoint, get back a 64-character IRN plus a signed QR code, and embed both on the customer-facing invoice. The complexity is in everything around that one call — strict schema validation, IRP sandbox quirks, and a 30-day hard cutoff for any business over ₹10 crore AATO. Keep those thresholds in config rather than hard-coding them: they reflect the rules as of late 2026, and GSTN has changed them several times before. Five IRPs currently handle this in production: NIC's free government portal, and four GSTN-approved private IRPs (ClearTax, Cygnet, IRIS, EY). Most serious integrations go through a GST Suvidha Provider (GSP) rather than hitting the IRP raw. If you're scoping this for a client or your own product, the real engineering work isn't the API call — it's the retry logic, idempotency handling, and a reconciliation layer that flags anything stuck in a pending or failed state before the 30-day window closes. title: Schema Markup for Local Businesses: The 5 Types That Actually Matter
author: Quicklity
summary: When someone searches for a plumber near them, a café that is open now, or a dentist with good reviews, Google does more than rank web pages. It tries to understand real businesses: where they are, when they are open, what they do, and what customers think of them. Schema markup is the structured data that helps search engines understand those facts. It is a small block of code, usually written in JSON-LD, that describes your business in a format machines can read easily. It does not change what visitors see on your page, but it can help Google show richer and more useful results. That does not mean every business needs every type of schema. For most local businesses, five types cover almost everything that matters. Start with those, get them right, and ignore the rest until you have a clear reason to add more. Why local businesses benefit Local search is competitive, and small details can make a difference. Clear LocalBusiness markup can help Google connect your website with your address, your service area, and your Google Business Profile. FAQ markup can make your answers eligible for expanded results. Review markup can make star ratings eligible to appear beside your listing. Breadcrumbs can make your pages easier to understand. None of this is guaranteed. Google decides which rich results to show, and when. Think of schema as giving Google accurate, well-organised information — not as a switch that forces a particular display. The benefit is better understanding, and better understanding can lead to better visibility in local results and the local pack. The golden rule: match what visitors can see Before choosing a type, remember one rule: your markup must match the content on the page. If your opening hours, address, prices, services, or reviews appear in your schema, visitors should be able to see the same information on that page. Do not add markup for services you do not offer, reviews you have not received, or opening hours that are not shown anywhere. If the markup and the visible page do not match, Google may ignore the markup — and repeated mismatches can damage trust in your site. 1. LocalBusiness This is the foundation for almost every local business. Use the most specific subtype that fits, such as Dentist, Restaurant, HairSalon, or Plumber, rather than the generic LocalBusiness type when a closer match exists. Include your business name, address, telephone number, website, and the area you serve. Keep these details identical everywhere they appear online, including your website, your Google Business Profile, and local directories. Small differences, such as a changed phone number or an old address, can confuse search engines. If you have more than one location, give each location its own page and its own LocalBusiness markup. One block that tries to describe several branches usually creates confusion rather than clarity. 2. FAQPage Many local business pages already answer common questions: how much does it cost, how do I book, is there parking, what is your cancellation policy? FAQPage markup can make those questions and answers eligible for rich results. Write the questions exactly as customers ask them, and keep each answer short and direct. Only mark up questions that are actually answered on the page, and do not use FAQ markup for advertising copy or for questions with no real answer. 3. Review and AggregateRating Reviews are powerful for local businesses, and schema can help search engines understand them. If genuine customers have reviewed your business, AggregateRating can summarise the average rating and the number of reviews. Individual Review markup can describe a specific customer's experience. Only use reviews that are real, visible on your site, and collected fairly. Never invent reviews, copy reviews from another site, or mark up testimonials that visitors cannot see. Google is strict about this, and fake review markup is one of the fastest ways to lose eligibility for rich results. 4. OpeningHoursSpecification OpeningHoursSpecification is part of LocalBusiness, but it deserves attention on its own. Include your regular weekly hours, and update them for bank holidays, seasonal changes, and temporary closures. "Open now" is one of the most useful signals in local search, so wrong hours are worse than no hours at all. If different parts of the business have different hours — for example, a shop and a phone line — describe them separately rather than merging them into one misleading timetable. 5. BreadcrumbList Breadcrumbs show the path to a page, such as Home > Services > Boiler Repairs. BreadcrumbList markup helps Google understand your site structure, and it can make search results easier to read. Keep the breadcrumb trail short, logical, and identical to the navigation visitors see. It is a small detail, but it helps both search engines and people understand where a page sits on your site. A short JSON-LD example Here is a simple example for a local café. Adapt the details to your own business, but keep the structure: { "@context" : "https://schema.org" , "@type" : "CafeOrCoffeeShop" , "name" : "Riverside Café" , "telephone" : "+44 20 7946 0000" , "address" : { "@type" : "PostalAddress" , "streetAddress" : "12 High Street" , "addressLocality" : "London" , "postalCode" : "SW1A 1AA" , "addressCountry" : "GB" }, "openingHoursSpecification" : { "@type" : "OpeningHoursSpecification" , "dayOfWeek" : [ "Monday" , "Tuesday" , "Wednesday" , "Thursday" , "Friday" ], "opens" : "08:00" , "closes" : "17:00" } } How to test your markup After adding schema, test the page with Google's Rich Results Test. Enter the URL, or paste the code, and check for errors and warnings. Fix errors first, then work through warnings where you can. Also check that the page still makes sense to a human visitor. The test tool can confirm that your code is valid, but it cannot confirm that your hours are correct or that your reviews are genuine. Test again after any change to your business details. Common mistakes to avoid Adding fake or copied reviews. Marking up content that is hidden from visitors. Using the wrong type — for example, marking a service business as a Product. Copying schema from another business and forgetting to change the name, address, or hours. Adding every schema type you can find, instead of the few that genuinely describe the page. Most of these mistakes come from rushing. Schema works best when it is accurate, specific, and honest about what the page actually offers. Start small, then build You do not need to add everything at once. Start with LocalBusiness, add your opening hours, then add FAQs, reviews, and breadcrumbs where they genuinely fit. Test each change, keep the visible page and the markup in agreement, and review them whenever your details change. If you want a quicker start, the free Schema Markup Generator at https://quicklitytools.com/schema-markup-generator can help you build valid JSON-LD without writing it from scratch. Check the output, adapt it to your real business details, and test it before you publish.

title: Building Introworth: A Modest Buffer Is a Metric, Not a Mood — What Worked, What Broke
author: OneLifeVibe
summary: The first version of this net-worth tracker showed a daily balance, and the daily balance was a liar. Not wrong, exactly — just unhelpful. It rose on payday, fell through the month, spiked when a card payment cleared, and dipped when rent left. A user could check it every morning for a month, feel alternately rich and doomed, and learn almost nothing about whether their position was actually improving. That failure shaped the rebuild. A household can end two different months on exactly the same balance and be in opposite positions: in one month a card balance quietly grew to cover the gap, in the other a modest cash buffer did. The headline number is identical. The direction is not. So the product stopped asking "what is the balance today?" and started asking "what changed since last month, and what absorbed the shocks?" Designing the snapshot Three choices shaped this part of the build. First, one snapshot on the same date each month, not a live feed. Assets and debts listed side by side, one honest total. A single month proves nothing; three months in a row show whether debts are shrinking, whether a buffer is forming, and whether a good month was progress or just timing. Second, the buffer is its own line, separate from everyday spending money. This turned out to be the most important field in the whole design. When a car repair or a higher utility bill lands on savings set aside for exactly that purpose, it is an inconvenience. When the same bill lands on a card, it becomes next month's problem as well, with interest attached. If the buffer is merged into the general balance, that difference is invisible until it is too late to act on. Third, the check-in has to be finishable in a few minutes. The habit the product supports is deliberately undramatic: one check-in, one honest total, one clear answer to whether the position moved forward. What worked The trend line beat the balance graph immediately. Users stopped reacting to payday spikes and started reacting to the three-month direction, which is the only signal in the data that reliably means anything. A flat month next to two rising months reads as a pause. The same flat month in the old daily view read as a crisis, because it usually followed a big bill day. The separate buffer line changed behaviour more than any chart did. People who could see the buffer as a number with a job — "this absorbs one bad month" — treated drawing on it as a decision instead of an accident, and refilling it became a concrete target with an end point rather than a vague intention to save more. Monthly cadence also fixed a data-quality problem nobody had predicted. When people update once a month, they reconcile. They check the card statement, notice the subscription that renewed, catch the account they forgot. Daily check-ins were mostly glances; monthly check-ins are audits, and the numbers got more honest as the cadence got slower. What broke, or nearly did The first snapshot form asked for too much. Fourteen fields, categories for every kind of asset, subtotals everywhere. Completion fell off a cliff — people would start the check-in, hit a field they did not know offhand, and abandon the whole month. A missing month breaks the trend line worse than an approximate one does. The form was cut to the totals that actually move the direction: what is owned, what is owed, and the buffer. Detail can live in the source apps; the snapshot only needs to be honest and repeatable. Double-counting the buffer was the subtlest bug, and it was a design bug, not a code bug. Early versions let the same savings appear both as an asset and as the buffer line, so net worth looked better whenever someone "built a buffer" by relabelling money they already had. The fix was boring and absolute: the buffer is a view of part of the assets, never an addition to them. Any metric that improves when you rename a thing will be gamed, usually by accident, always at the worst moment. Irregular income broke the "same date" rule for a while. Freelancers and shift workers do not have a payday-shaped month, and a snapshot taken before a late invoice landed made their trend look worse than it was. The rule now is "same point in your cycle," not the same calendar date — consistency of position matters more than consistency of the number on the calendar. Lessons for builders Pick the cadence that makes the data honest, not the cadence that makes the chart lively. For money direction, monthly and reconciled beats daily and glanced, every time. Give the protective number its own line. A buffer that is not separately visible does not change behaviour, because nobody can tell the month it quietly saved them. Never let a derived metric be addable to its own source. If relabelling money can improve the score, the score is measuring labels. Design the check-in for the worst month, not the best one. The month someone least wants to open the app is the month the trend line most needs. The project behind these lessons is Introworth , where assets and debts are tracked together in one monthly view, the buffer is tracked as its own line, and the trend — not a single day's balance — is the answer the product gives.

title: The real bottleneck in AI video upscaling is temporal consistency, not resolution
author: celticgemini001
summary: Everyone benchmarks upscalers on a single still frame. That is the easy part. Run the same model across 300 consecutive frames and the output starts to boil : edges crawl, texture shimmers, and grain that was static in the source starts dancing. Why per-frame inference fails A neural upscaler is a function f(frame) -> bigger frame . Applied frame by frame, it has no idea that frame 41 and frame 42 depict the same wall. Small differences in the model's prediction — a slightly different interpretation of a shadow — become visible as flicker precisely because the rest of the image is stable. The fix is either: Optical-flow guided warping — propagate the previous frame's high-res result forward along motion vectors, then only infer the residual. Temporal conditioning — feed the model several adjacent frames so it predicts a consistent sequence rather than independent stills. Both are expensive. This is also why consumer upscalers cap video length: the cost per second is an order of magnitude above stills. What to do about it as a user Prefer shorter clips. Temporal artefacts accumulate over long sequences. Denoise before upscaling. Noise is the single biggest driver of frame-to-frame inconsistency — if the model interprets random grain differently each frame, you get shimmer that no amount of temporal smoothing can fix afterwards. Compare output playing , never paused. A paused frame hides exactly the defect you are trying to evaluate. I have been testing this with UpgoLAB , which does video upscaling server-side in the browser — free during its launch period, no install. The practical limit it hits is exactly this cost curve, not image quality. The takeaway If you are evaluating an upscaler on stills alone, you are evaluating the easy 20% of the problem. Motion is where the engineering actually lives.

title: Your Listing Is a Snapshot, Not a Contract
author: minia2a
summary: This content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only , 5 free trial calls per signed wallet , no credits and no top-up rail. 2026-11-09 · x402 operations A buyer finds your endpoint in a discovery index. The index shows a price, a payee address, a chain. Where did those three values come from, and how old are they? For x402scan, the answer is specific: at registration . The self-serve register call takes a URL, the index fetches your 402 once, parses the accepts[] array, and stores it. Nothing re-probes that row afterwards. Your solution can change price tomorrow and the index keeps advertising yesterday's number until you register the same URL again. We measured how much that matters for us. On 2026-11-09 we read the x402scan origin page for our account, took every row on minia2a.uk , and probed each URL against the live challenge to compare four things: the atomic amount, the payee, the rail (network + asset), and whether the URL still answers 402 at all. The population measurement value rows under minia2a.uk 1,123 snapshot age, median 0 days snapshot age, max 65 days rows older than 30 days 113 rows older than 45 days 70 accepts per row 1 (all 1,123) Two things stand out. First, the median age is zero — most of our rows were registered recently, which is what a healthy self-serve flow looks like. Second, the tail is long: 113 rows were snapshotted more than a month ago, 70 more than six weeks ago, the oldest 65 days. Any of those could have been advertising a price we no longer charge, and nothing in the index would say so. The result verdict rows identical to the live 402 1,122 price or payee drift 0 dead (no 402, no explanation) 0 retired (404 that names a replacement) 1 transient / unusable 0 Not one row was wrong. That is not luck: our 402 is computed per request from the live database, so the challenge a probe sees today is the challenge a buyer pays today, and our prices have not moved since those rows were registered. The stale snapshots are stale in date only — the values inside them still agree with the server. That is exactly the shape of a latent bug. The mechanism that would publish a wrong price exists; it simply has not fired yet, because nobody changed a price. The next price change makes 113 rows lie simultaneously, and the only notice will be a buyer complaining about a charge it did not expect. The one dead row https://minia2a.uk/x402/language-detect returns 404. We delisted that service because it answered "english" for every Latin-script language — French, German, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese all came back English after a confident-looking detection pass. A 404 is a fine answer to a probe. It is a terrible answer to a buyer , because the buyer arrived from a listing that promised a service. So the 404 body carries the explanation and the replacement: { "delisted" : true , "error" : "Service not found" , "id" : "language-detect" , "hint" : "language-detect delisted — it answered \" english \" for every Latin-script language ... Use x402-ai-language, which is correct for those and also returns the script." } Whoever follows that dead row lands on a live endpoint that does the job. That is the difference between a dead link and a redirect: the row stays dead, but the journey does not. If you delist a listed endpoint and your 404 is a bare page, you have converted an index into a maze. The trap in checking whether you are listed x402scan writes rows through two paths, and they land in different buckets: self-serve register writes method: "" discovery (from your openapi.json ) writes method: "GET" or "POST" The registration check is keyed on (url, method) . So asking "is this URL registered?" with one method and calling it a day under-reports — and under-reporting is the direction that makes you register everything a second time. Our own measurements of the same account, on the same day, across three methods: query registered GET only 29 of 105 GET + POST 16 of 132 GET + POST + "" 89 of 132 The first two numbers were both wrong, and the second was lower than the first despite asking about more endpoints — a bigger population with an incomplete union. Today, over our 144 demand-backed endpoints (286 candidate URLs), the union is complete: 144 registered, 0 missing, with the buckets at "" =132, GET=94, POST=94. What we did not do 1,123 of our 1,856 catalog services are in that index; 733 are not. Some of the 733 have never taken a single call. We did not mass-register them. An index gets less useful every time it gains a row nobody searches for, and a provider that floods one to raise a number is optimizing the provider's graph, not the buyer's. Discovery is a shared resource; spam spends it. Limits of this audit One index, one provider, one day. x402scan stores registration snapshots; CDP's Bazaar files a row from the payment payload at settle time, so its rows are settle snapshots with a different freshness mechanism and a different failure mode. The live probe is an unpaid GET . It proves the challenge — price, payee, chain, liveness — is current. It does not prove a payment settles, and it does not test delivery. lastUpdated is when the row was registered, not when it was last verified. A fresh date is not evidence the row was re-read. Snapshot age and correctness are independent. All 113 stale rows happened to be correct. That is a fact about our changelog, not a property of the index. The rule A listing is a photograph of your 402 taken by someone else. The 402 is the contract. If you cannot make the index notice that the contract changed, you owe it — and your buyers — a scheduled re-read of the photograph. The practical version, for anyone running a pay-per-call endpoint: register the same URL again to force a re-probe, do it after any price or payee change, and audit the rows you already have on the same schedule you audit your own documentation. And make sure a dead row points somewhere alive — the index will keep the dead link for as long as it likes. Originally published at minia2a.uk .

title: AI Consulting Services for Business Strategy and Growth
author: Raja Kumar
summary: Businesses in Singapore are increasingly exploring AI to improve productivity, automate repetitive activities and support better decisions. Effective ai strategy consulting also considers the organisation's existing infrastructure, data availability, security requirements and employee readiness. What to Evaluate Before Adopting AI A successful AI project begins with understanding the organisation's current business environment. The following areas can help businesses assess their readiness. 1. Business requirements and objectives Identify the operational challenges that AI should address. These may include repetitive administrative work, slow customer response times, manual reporting or difficulties accessing internal information. Clear objectives help businesses select applications that solve actual problems. 2. Existing technology and infrastructure Review the software and systems currently used across departments. Businesses should understand whether their existing infrastructure can support new AI applications or requires additional development and configuration. 3. Data availability and readiness AI applications depend on relevant and reliable information. Organisations should evaluate where their data is stored, how it is maintained and whether it can be accessed securely by the proposed applications. 4. Security and governance requirements Businesses must establish how information will be accessed, processed and protected. Access permissions, data handling policies and human supervision should be considered before connecting AI applications to internal systems. 5. Employee readiness and technical capabilities Employees need to understand how AI tools fit into their responsibilities. Organisations should also evaluate whether their internal IT teams have the expertise required to manage and maintain the applications. These assessments provide a practical foundation for technology selection. They also help management understand the investment, resources and organisational changes required before implementation. Common AI Adoption Challenges Businesses Face Although AI can support different business activities, organisations may encounter practical difficulties when introducing it into existing operations. These challenges often arise when businesses lack a clear plan or underestimate the work required to prepare their systems. Two areas require particular attention when planning AI adoption. Planning AI Adoption Without Disrupting Existing Operations Businesses need to introduce AI without creating unnecessary changes to their daily activities. Employees should be able to use new applications while continuing to manage their regular responsibilities. A gradual approach helps organisations test applications and understand their impact before expanding adoption. Identifying suitable opportunities: Review existing processes to find repetitive activities where AI can provide practical support. Managing business workflows: Understand how new AI applications will affect the responsibilities of different departments. Preparing internal data: Organise relevant business information and ensure it is suitable for the intended AI application. Selecting appropriate technologies: Evaluate available models and tools based on business requirements, security and technical capabilities. Allocating technical resources: Determine the infrastructure, expertise and ongoing support needed to manage AI applications. These activities help businesses establish realistic priorities before starting development. Management should also involve employees who understand the existing workflows and can provide useful feedback during testing. Connecting AI With Existing Business Systems Many organisations already depend on CRM, ERP, HRMS and customer support platforms to manage their operations. Introducing AI without considering these systems can create disconnected applications and additional manual work. Businesses should understand how information moves between platforms before planning integration. CRM connectivity: Allow suitable AI applications to access approved customer information and support sales activities. ERP integration: Explore how AI can assist with retrieving operational information and supporting internal processes. HRMS connectivity: Support employee-related information access and routine HR activities through approved systems. Customer support integration: Help support teams retrieve relevant information and prepare responses to common enquiries. Data access management: Establish permissions and controls to determine which applications and users can access specific information. Integration planning should consider the technical requirements of each platform. Businesses must also establish appropriate security controls and decide which actions require human approval. How to Develop an Effective AI Implementation Strategy After identifying suitable opportunities, organisations need a practical plan to move from evaluation to deployment. An ai implementation strategy connects business requirements with technology selection, development, testing and ongoing management. For example, a company may begin with an internal AI assistant that helps employees find information from approved documents. Once the application has been tested and its performance evaluated, the organisation may consider extending it to other departments. A well-planned ai implementation strategy helps businesses manage this process in stages. Businesses should begin with clearly defined objectives and select applications that can be tested within a manageable scope. This makes it easier to identify technical limitations and understand whether the solution is delivering the expected results. Performance measurement is another important part of the process. Organisations can evaluate response accuracy, processing time, employee adoption and the reduction of repetitive work. These indicators help management decide whether further improvements or additional investment are necessary. A flexible ai implementation strategy also allows businesses to adjust their approach as requirements change. Regular reviews and employee feedback can help ensure that AI applications remain relevant to operational needs. Evaluating AI Integration Requirements Before Implementation AI applications often need to work with multiple business platforms to provide useful results. ai integration consulting helps organisations assess how these applications can connect with existing software, databases and internal workflows. Each connection must be planned according to the application's purpose and access requirements. ai integration consulting can help evaluate these connections and identify technical requirements before deployment. Businesses should also consider application programming interfaces (APIs), authentication methods, data formats and system compatibility. These technical factors influence how easily AI applications can communicate with existing platforms. Security should remain part of the integration process. Organisations must define access permissions, monitor information exchange and ensure that sensitive records are available only to authorised users. Before deployment, businesses should test the connections under realistic conditions. This helps identify errors, performance limitations and permission issues before employees begin using the applications. ai integration consulting can also help businesses assess whether the connected systems meet their operational and security requirements.
