title: Kabilio closes €10M round to launch AI accounting agent
author: Mikhail Savchenko
summary: Spanish fintech Kabilio has raised €10 million, according to Tech.eu . Picus Capital and Visionaries led the round, and CDTI, Spain's public agency for technological innovation, took part. Both lead investors also backed the earlier pre-seed round. Total funding since launch is now €14 million. What Kabilio sells The platform targets accounting firms and the small businesses they serve. In Spain and much of Europe, small companies commonly hand bookkeeping and tax work to outside firms, which then process large volumes of invoices, bank transactions and documents, often with manual input and reconciliation. Kabilio's software reads invoices, proposes accounting entries, matches bank transactions, prepares reconciliations and flags the cases that need a professional's attention. It runs next to the software a firm already uses, and accountants review and approve instead of typing. The company says this cuts time spent on bookkeeping and reconciliation by about 60 per cent. That figure is the company's own claim, not an independent measurement. The agent The new element is an AI accounting agent. It is meant to handle tasks such as fetching invoices, reconciling transactions, validating entries and asking for missing documents by email and WhatsApp. Accountants give it instructions in plain language and decide how much autonomy it has. Several firms are piloting it now. Kabilio has also launched Kabilio Empresas, a platform where small businesses issue invoices, connect bank accounts and watch cash flow, while sharing the data with their accounting firm in real time. Fiscalidad Inteligente and Alemany Assessors use it for a large part of their client portfolios. Co-founder and co-CEO Álex Valls put the logic this way: an agent depends on the quality of its data, so the firm's clients are being brought onto the same platform. When a client issues an invoice or a payment arrives, the firm sees it and the agent can act. What comes next A later phase would extend the agent to the small business clients themselves. The plan is for it to issue invoices, chase overdue payments, ask for missing receipts and answer routine accounting and tax questions. The source gives no date for this phase. Scale Kabilio says it works with nearly 500 accounting firms, up from 100 a year ago. Named customers include Adlanter, Solfico and Gemap, the last two part of the iusTime group. The team has grown to 80 people, more than half in product and engineering. The new money will fund the agent rollout, more workflow automation and the shared platform for firms and their clients.

title: AI Compute Just Hit a Political Ceiling
author: Max Quimby
summary: The AI industry modeled every supply constraint except one: democracy. 📖 Read the full version with charts and embedded sources on ComputeLeap → On November 6, market-intelligence firm Cleanview published an analysis that should have sent shockwaves through every AI infrastructure investor's portfolio: 41% of planned US data center capacity — 158.6 gigawatts — sits in states where newly elected governors have pledged to pause or halt construction. Nine states. Nearly half the pipeline. Not delayed by supply-chain bottlenecks or permitting friction, but by elected officials who campaigned on stopping the buildout. This is not a zoning dispute. It is a structural political constraint on AI compute supply that nobody's discounted cash flow model accounted for. SK Ventures General Partner Paul Kedrosky broke down the implications in a video for The Information: slower construction means revenue shortfalls and delivery delays for Nvidia and every company downstream of GPU silicon. ARK Invest's Cathie Wood went further on her "In The Know" segment, calling the political backlash "real and underpriced" — a remarkable admission from someone whose models depend on exponential compute scaling. ℹ️ The 41% figure: Cleanview estimates 158.6 GW of planned US data center capacity sits in states where newly elected governors pledged construction pauses. Texas alone accounts for 88.4 GW. Ohio adds 21.9 GW, Georgia 20.2 GW, New Mexico 11 GW, and New York 9.9 GW. The math that should worry you Here is what 41% actually means in practice. The United States has roughly 386 gigawatts of data center capacity in various stages of planning. Of that, 56.7 GW is already under construction — those projects will likely proceed regardless of who sits in the governor's mansion. But the remaining pipeline, the capacity that hyperscalers need to meet 2027-2028 demand projections, is heavily concentrated in states that just elected leaders hostile to the buildout. Texas leads the exposure at 88.4 GW — more than every other at-risk state combined. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned explicitly on pausing data center deals, telling HuffPost : "That stops when I'm governor." She also requested an immediate pause on land talks with SpaceX , signaling that the posture extends beyond data centers to the entire tech-land complex in Texas. This is not just Texas. Ohio, Georgia, Michigan, and New Mexico all elected governors who ran on construction pauses. New York and Oregon pledged to extend pauses already in place. Iowa and Nevada's incoming governors want to end AI tax breaks entirely. Florida's incoming governor proposed requiring data centers to generate their own electricity rather than draw from the grid. View original post on Reddit → The scale of the shift is unprecedented. According to Seaport analyst Jay Goldberg , only about 30 of 55 gigawatts announced for 2027 will actually get built — a 45% shortfall even before accounting for the political wave. Add the governor pauses, and the gap widens dramatically. This was building for years The November ballot didn't create this opposition. It crystallized it. We covered the early warning signs in our July deep-dive on AI's water bill and the data center backlash , when Meta's Cheyenne facility contaminated a city's water supply and communities across the country started organizing. Since then, the numbers have only gotten worse. By March 2026, active data center opposition groups had more than doubled to 833 across 49 states . A Heatmap Pro/Embold Research poll found that 75% of registered US voters oppose data center construction near their homes — up from 57% just eighteen months ago. Gallup identified excessive water usage as the top reason for opposition. A Harvard Gazette analysis documented how the opposition crosses political lines in ways that are unusual in American politics. The financial toll has been staggering. In Q1 2026 alone, community opposition delayed or blocked at least 75 projects worth approximately $130 billion, the largest single-quarter concentration on record . By Q2, another 45 projects worth $68 billion were disrupted. What changed in November is that this grassroots opposition found its political vehicle. Candidates ran on it. And they won. What the community is saying Reddit's r/technology lit up with the results. The post "Americans just resoundingly rejected AI data centers" pulled 4,558 upvotes and 179 comments, with users pointing out that this was the first election cycle where data centers were a defining ballot issue. View original post on Reddit → The Texas threads were even bigger. The governor-elect's warning to Big Tech drew 8,233 upvotes and 350 comments , while the SpaceX land-deal pause hit 18,630 upvotes . The comment threads reveal a seam of working-class frustration: residents who watched their electricity bills spike, their water bills climb, and their property values stagnate while data centers got tax breaks. On X, the backlash generated its own counter-backlash. Nikita Bier's tweet calling out anti-data-center politicians went viral with 21,518 likes and 745K views: "If any elected leader opposes data centers or the reindustrialization of America, just say you support them in Chinese." View original post on X → The framing — that opposing data centers is opposing American competitiveness — resonated in tech circles but clearly failed to carry the electorate. Meanwhile, Chamath Palihapitiya offered the economic meta-narrative in a tweet that pulled 4,008 likes and 558K views: "The American economy has decoupled the economic progress of asset owners from wage earners." The data center backlash, in Chamath's framing, is a symptom of a deeper economic resentment — communities watching tech companies extract resources while the benefits flow upward. View original post on X → The Nvidia transmission mechanism If you own Nvidia stock — or anything downstream of GPU demand — this is where you should pay attention. Nvidia's own filings have warned that infrastructure shortages could delay chip purchases and hurt revenue . The CFO said the supply-demand gap is expected to remain a bottleneck through fiscal year 2028. But those warnings were about engineering constraints: transformer lead times, grid capacity, skilled labor shortages. The political dimension is different because it is not solvable with money. You can throw capital at a transformer shortage and eventually get more transformers built. You cannot throw capital at a governor who campaigned on stopping your project. The political constraint operates on a different timeline and responds to different incentives than engineering constraints. As Trefis noted in May : "The grid, not chip supply, is now the main constraint." After November, we should amend that: the grid and the ballot box. We analyzed Nvidia's dual role as chipmaker and financial backstop in our piece on Nvidia as the central bank of AI . The political constraint adds a new risk: if the data centers those chips are destined for cannot be built, Nvidia's compute-as-commodity thesis faces a supply crunch from an entirely unexpected direction. The supply-side tell: NVKE and the "optimize what you have" play One data point from GitHub Trending tells the supply-side story in miniature. NVKE (NVIDIA Kubernetes Engine) , a management plane for running GPU Kubernetes on bare metal, gained +345 stars in a single day this week. Why does a bare-metal GPU orchestration tool suddenly spike? Because when you cannot build new data centers, you squeeze more out of existing ones. NVKE strips the virtualization overhead to run workloads directly on GPU hardware — the infrastructure equivalent of fuel rationing. This is the pattern to watch. As political constraints bind, the value migrates from "build more" to "use better." Companies that can extract more compute per watt from existing facilities gain a structural advantage over those whose business models assume infinite buildout capacity. ⚠️ Contrarian Corner: Campaign pledges are not enacted policy. Governors cannot unilaterally halt construction — they need legislatures, and many of these states have divided governments. The 41% figure may be a negotiation opener: governors horse-trade pauses for concessions (water treatment upgrades, local hiring requirements, tax revenue sharing). The historical pattern with industrial pushback is accommodation, not permanent ban. Maine tried to ban data centers outright and failed. The buildout may simply shift to friendlier states — Alabama, Tennessee, and the Carolinas are already courting displaced projects. The contrarian case is real, but it has a timing problem. Even if every governor-elect eventually negotiates a deal, the delay itself is costly. Data center construction takes 18-36 months. A six-month pause for policy negotiation pushes delivery into 2028-2029 for projects that hyperscalers needed in 2027. In a demand environment where enterprise AI adoption is accelerating, delay is not neutral — it compounds. What this means for you If you are building AI products: Compute costs will stay elevated longer than consensus expects. Budget accordingly. If your architecture assumes cheap inference at scale by mid-2027, revisit that assumption. Optimize for efficiency now — smaller models, better caching, smarter routing — rather than counting on supply expansion to bring costs down. If you are investing in AI infrastructure: The risk profile just changed. Nvidia, Vertiv, Eaton, and the electrical-infrastructure stack now carry unpriced political risk alongside their engineering risk. The stocks that benefit are efficiency plays: companies that help extract more from existing capacity rather than build new. If you are a policy maker or community leader: The leverage is real but perishable. The window for negotiating meaningful concessions — water treatment, grid upgrades, local hiring, revenue sharing — is now. Once the federal government moves to pre-empt state moratoria (and it will — President Trump has already argued that blocking data centers is a mistake), the negotiating position weakens. 💡 The builder's playbook: (1) Audit your compute-per-watt efficiency — there is likely 20-40% headroom in most deployments. (2) Diversify hosting across geographies, weighting toward politically stable jurisdictions. (3) Build cost models that assume 18-month political delays on new capacity. (4) Watch NVKE-style tools — the "optimize existing" stack is where alpha lives in a constrained-supply world. The deeper pattern Step back from the data center specifics and a larger pattern emerges. The AI industry's "build first, ask permission never" era is ending. It ended not because regulators caught up or because the technology hit a wall, but because voters in nine states decided that the externalities — the water, the electricity bills, the noise, the tax breaks — were no longer acceptable. This is the AI industry's first real encounter with democratic accountability. It will not be the last. The 41% number will likely come down as governors negotiate and some pauses prove temporary. But the political ceiling — the idea that AI compute supply growth now requires democratic consent, not just capital — is permanent. Every future data center project in America will now account for community opposition as a first-order constraint, not an afterthought. The industry that talks endlessly about scaling laws just discovered a new one: political gravity scales, too. Originally published at ComputeLeap

title: Why Cometflow Do Will Be a Life-Changing Software
author: Pratyush Ranjan Roul
summary: What if you didn't have to search for the right tool every time you wanted to get something done? What if you could simply describe your task, and your device understood what you meant, figured out the steps, and helped you complete the work? That is the idea behind Cometflow Do. We are building Cometflow Do around a simple belief: software should adapt to people, not force people to learn complicated interfaces. The Problem With Today's Software Think about an ordinary day. You need to convert some images into a PDF. You search for a website, upload your images, wait for processing, download the result, and repeat the process next time. Then you need to compress a file, calculate something, clean up text, organize information, or prepare a document. Each task takes you through a different application, website, interface, and workflow. Individually, these tools might be useful. But collectively, they create friction. People spend too much time figuring out how to perform a task instead of actually completing it. We believe there is a better approach. Introducing Cometflow Do Cometflow Do is a native Android application being developed as a privacy-first utility and action platform. It is not designed to be just another chatbot. Its long-term vision is to become a Personal Action Engine: a system that connects natural-language instructions with useful, real operations. Instead of browsing through categories and searching for individual utilities, users should eventually be able to describe what they need in their own words. For example: Convert these JPEG images into one PDF. Remove duplicate entries from this text. Compress these images before sharing. Calculate the percentage of these numbers. Prepare a study schedule for my upcoming exams. The application aims to understand the request, identify the appropriate functionality, and execute the task. More Than 500 Tools Built Across the Ecosystem One of the major parts of Cometflow Do is its growing utility ecosystem. More than 500 tools have been built across its development stages, covering different everyday and digital workflows. These include areas such as: Image and document processing Text transformation and analysis Developer utilities Calculations and converters File operations Productivity and everyday tasks Privacy-oriented utilities However, the number of tools is not the ultimate goal. A large collection of utilities means very little if users cannot discover them easily or trust their results. Our focus is making these capabilities accessible through a simpler experience and improving execution reliability. The Intent Engine: Making Software Understand People This is one of the most important parts of our vision. Traditional utility applications expect users to know the name of a tool and provide input in a specific format. We want to reduce that dependency. We are working towards an intent-understanding architecture that can interpret natural-language commands, handle common typing mistakes, understand incomplete instructions, and use conversational context. Consider this interaction: User: Apple, mango, banana, apple. User: Remove duplicates. The application should understand that the second instruction refers to the previous text. This requires more than keyword matching. It requires intent detection, context handling, tool discovery, clarification, and reliable execution. Our proposed architecture uses local processing and the existing native Kotlin utility ecosystem as its foundation. From Individual Tools to Complete Workflows Another important part of Cometflow Do's future is multi-step execution. Imagine saying: "Prepare these images for sharing." Instead of manually opening multiple utilities, the application could eventually coordinate a workflow: Resize the selected images. Compress them. Rename the output files. Package them into a ZIP archive. Save the final result. This is the difference between providing access to tools and helping someone complete a task. We want Cometflow Do to move towards the second approach. Why Privacy Matters We believe everyday utility operations should not always require cloud-based AI services. Basic operations such as text processing, calculations, encoding, and many file transformations can be performed directly on the device. Our development direction prioritizes: Local-first processing. No mandatory account for everyday utility usage. No requirement for paid AI APIs to execute basic utilities. Optional offline intelligence where device resources allow. Transparent file operations and permissions. The objective is to make useful software accessible without making users dependent on expensive services. Built for Real People, Not Just Technology Enthusiasts Cometflow Do is intended for people with different needs. A student might use it to calculate marks, organize study material, or prepare documents. A creator might use it to process images and manage content-related tasks. A developer might use its text, data, and coding utilities. An everyday user might simply want to convert a file or complete a repetitive task. The interface should not make users understand the underlying technology before they can benefit from it. They should just explain what they want to accomplish. Why We Think This Could Be Life-Changing We are not claiming that one application will solve every problem. But we believe removing small, repeated frustrations from everyday digital work can make a meaningful difference. Saving a few steps every day matters. Not having to search for another website matters. Being able to complete a task without understanding a complicated interface matters. And having more control over your data matters. The real opportunity is not building another application with hundreds of buttons. It is changing how people interact with software. The Road Ahead Cometflow Do is still evolving. We are continuing to improve utility reliability, natural-language understanding, contextual assistance, file workflows, and offline capabilities. Our ambition is to build software that does not merely tell people how to complete tasks, but helps them actually complete those tasks. Cometflow Do is being built around one simple idea: Tell the software what you want done, not which tool you want to use. That is the future we are working towards. What would you want an application like this to do for you?

title: The benchmark wrote it in its own headline: Korea's Darwin on the board for the first time
author: AI OpenFree
summary: Read the headline, not just the score Benchmark news is usually read through the score. This one should be read through the headline. At 19:53 on 4 November 2026, SuperCLUE published its November monthly evaluation. The author is the SuperCLUE team and the channel is the official CLUE Chinese Language Understanding Evaluation account. Its headline reads: "November 2026 Chinese large model benchmark results released! Kimi-K3.1-Pro #1 in China, Korean model Darwin on the board for the first time! " That is a translation of the Chinese original, which closes with the phrase for "on the board for the first time". There were two slots in that headline. One went to China's top-scoring model. The other came to us. Out of 19 entrants, the party that chose which model to name in the headline was the party that did the scoring. This was not a press release we sent, and not our summary of someone else's table. The evaluator put our model's name in its own headline. The scoring design the announcement disclosed The announcement published this round's weights as numbers, which shows exactly which capability it valued. Task Weight Agentic coding 30% Math and science reasoning 24% Hallucination control 18% Precise instruction following 18% Ultra-long context 10% This round put the most weight on agentic coding, with math and science reasoning second. In the announcement's own words, that axis "emphasises logical derivation and quantitative analysis". All 19 models sat the same private exam under the same weights. What happened on the hardest axis The announcement reports the math and science reasoning result like this: "GPT-6.1-Sol leads the math and science reasoning board with 76.32, Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 (73.68) takes second , and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 and Gemini-4-Argon tie for third at 71.05" Second of 19. The gap to first is 2.64 points. Below us on that axis sit Gemini-4-Argon, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Grok-4.7 and Qwen3.8-Max-0902. Among open-weight models it is first. Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is the only Korean model on the board. The footnote written only for Darwin One more line in the announcement applies to our model alone. It appears in the cost-efficiency section. "*Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is an open-source deployed model, so API pricing and cost are not tallied. The open-source address is available at https://huggingface.co/FINAL-Bench/Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 " Two things follow from that footnote. First, the other leading models on the board have their cost efficiency computed from API pricing, and ours is not in that calculation at all. A model you pay per call to use and a model whose weights you download and run on your own hardware sit on entirely different cost axes. Second, the evaluator linked our repository directly in the body of its own announcement, so a reader who sees the score can fetch the weights immediately. It shares the board with its parent model Darwin-180B-RSI is a 180 billion parameter mixture-of-experts model with roughly 3 billion active per token. It inherited its 512 routed experts per layer from Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next byte for byte and rebuilt only the attention layers, the linear attention and the shared experts through recursive self-improvement: the model writes problems, solves them, verifies the answers and updates its own weights from the verified traces. Both models are on this board, so the comparison is direct. Qwen3.8-Flash Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 Math and science reasoning 57.89 73.68 Overall index 39.81 (15th) 43.08 (9th) Same stored knowledge, rebuilt reasoning path: 15.79 points on the hardest axis and six places on the overall index. Why this document is different Secondary coverage of the same result already exists. NetEase ran it on 7 November as "Second at 73.68, the open-weight model that left Gemini and Grok behind", and in Korea, ChosunBiz, Economist, Digital Daily and AI Times all reported it on 6 November within hours of each other. This announcement is the source those pieces drew from. It is the primary document, written by the party that produced the numbers, and the choice of headline was theirs too. Us saying "first among open-weight models" and the evaluator writing "Korean model Darwin on the board for the first time" are the same fact carrying different weight. Where to check it and what you can run The announcement is published here , and the full board is at superclueai.com . The weights are at Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 under the Qwen community licence with commercial use permitted, and the 4-bit on-device build POCKET-Darwin-180B-GGUF runs from SSD on a 32GB laptop. FAQ Who produced these scores? SuperCLUE, on its private November 2026 test set. VIDRAFT is an evaluated model on that board, not the operator of the benchmark. What does "on the board for the first time" mean? It means a Korean model appeared on the SuperCLUE board for the first time. The headline uses the Chinese phrase meaning "appears on the board for the first time". How do the two models in the headline relate? Kimi-K3.1-Pro is first among Chinese models with an overall index of 61.46, and Darwin-180B-RSI-R3 is second of 19 on math and science reasoning at 73.68, first among open-weight models. The announcement put both facts in one headline. Is Darwin first overall? It is first among open-weight models and second of 19 on math and science reasoning. On the displayed overall index it is 9th of 19 and 5th among open-weight models. What licence covers the weights? Qwen Community Licence 1.0, inherited from the model whose expert layers it reuses. Commercial use is permitted.
